title: Defending the data application
goals: Defend an application using reproducible evidence
Demonstrate a new case without hidden help

prerequisite.prompt: What makes a project result reproducible?
prerequisite.answer: Identified inputs, code/configuration, rules and expected outputs that another person can rerun.

vocabulary: An explanation supported by evidence and questions
The records needed to check a project claim
Showing the application on specified inputs
Giving another person enough information to use or check the work

blocks.text: Finish the fictional activity chooser with a short evidence-based presentation and a reproducible handover. Show the purpose, contract, pipeline, one ordinary trace, one boundary or failure case, improvements and remaining limits. A working demonstration supports a software claim, not a claim of proven learning benefit.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
report = {"supplied": 4, "accepted": 3, "rejected": 1,
          "eligible": 2, "selected": "A", "score": 8}
assert report["accepted"] + report["rejected"] == report["supplied"]
assert report["eligible"] <= report["accepted"]
print(report["selected"], report["score"])

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The example report prints A 8 and its counts are internally consistent. These checks do not prove A is the correct winner; the input records and scoring trace are also needed. Keep raw fictional data, source code, settings, test results and change log together.

blocks.label: A demonstration shows only the winning name. Name two pieces of evidence needed to explain that choice.

blocks.text: A polished presentation can conceal missing evidence. Replace claims such as works for everyone with the exact requirements met, cases executed and known limitations. Show one prior failure and its repair rather than deleting it from the story.

The final independent task must be attempted before hints. Record support honestly and use a new case after support. Keep teacher answers separate from student materials and do not publish private credentials or real student records in the handover.

blocks.label: After passing the new case, what remains unproven and what is a reasonable next step?

workbook.title: Assemble evidence
workbook.prompt: List the files or records a peer needs to reproduce the chooser result.
workbook.answer: Fictional raw dataset, schema, code version, settings, run instructions, tests with expected/actual results, rejection reasons and change log.

workbook.title: Check report consistency
workbook.prompt: A report says supplied 5, accepted 4 and rejected 2. Identify the inconsistency.
workbook.answer: Accepted plus rejected is 6, not 5. Investigate double counting or reporting before presenting it.

workbook.title: Repair a claim
workbook.prompt: A presentation says the project proves students learn better. What claim does a successful rule-based demo support instead?
workbook.answer: It supports that the tested version follows specified selection rules on the tested cases. Learning benefit needs separate classroom evidence.

workbook.title: Defend a new case independently
workbook.prompt: Limit is 10. A has minutes 10, fun 2, learning 4; B has 9,3,2; C has 11,5,5; D has 8,"4",2. Validate, rank, give counts, explain the winner, then reverse the input order. Present without hints.
workbook.answer: 4 supplied, 3 accepted, 1 rejected D for rating type, 2 eligible A/B. Both score 8; A wins alphabetically. C is valid but over-limit. Reversal preserves counts and A. Explain the policy and its limits.

workbook.title: State the next evidence need
workbook.prompt: After passing the new case, what remains unproven and what is a reasonable next step?
workbook.answer: All possible input correctness and educational benefit remain unproven. Add varied independent cases or propose a teacher-approved usability pilot with a defined question; do not claim outcomes before collecting evidence.

teacher.background: Teach Week 36 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. Finish the fictional activity chooser with a short evidence-based presentation and a reproducible handover. Show the purpose, contract, pipeline, one ordinary trace, one boundary or failure case, improvements and remaining limits. A working demonstration supports a software claim, not a claim of proven learning benefit. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.
materials: Python 3 editor with a fresh local practice file
Paper trace table and the student workbook
Fictional input records from this lesson; no real student identifiers
sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and explain the purpose in the opening section.
Read the worked example and diagram; ask learners to trace each step aloud.
Complete W1 and W2, then compare predictions with observed results.
Collect the guided prediction before running; discuss a mismatch and its cause.
Retrieve the main rule without showing the previous answer.
Use W3 to diagnose and repair the stated failure; rerun an earlier case.
Collect W4 independently, including code or plan, predictions and explanations, before hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit; use the fresh retry when support was needed.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The input records and eligibility/scoring/tie trace; also show the policy/version and rejection counts. Exit: All possible input correctness and educational benefit remain unproven. Add varied independent cases or propose a teacher-approved usability pilot with a defined question; do not claim outcomes before collecting evidence.
misconceptions: A successful run proves the conclusion

The final independent task must be attempted before hints. Record support honestly and use a new case after support. Keep teacher answers separate from student materials and do not publish private credentials or real student records in the handover.

Require the new W4 case, explicit predictions and an explanation. Fresh retry after support: limit 12; M (minutes 12, fun 3, learning 3), N (11,4,1), O (13,5,5), P (10,-1,2). Counts 4 supplied,3 accepted,1 rejected,2 eligible. M/N tie at 9; M wins in either order.

A polished presentation can conceal missing evidence. Replace claims such as works for everyone with the exact requirements met, cases executed and known limitations. Show one prior failure and its repair rather than deleting it from the story.
teacher.assessment: Independent W4 evidence: 4 supplied, 3 accepted, 1 rejected D for rating type, 2 eligible A/B. Both score 8; A wins alphabetically. C is valid but over-limit. Reversal preserves counts and A. Explain the policy and its limits. Record whether the learner needed no help, a hint or explanation. Fresh retry after support: limit 12; M (minutes 12, fun 3, learning 3), N (11,4,1), O (13,5,5), P (10,-1,2). Counts 4 supplied,3 accepted,1 rejected,2 eligible. M/N tie at 9; M wins in either order.
teacher.support: Offer a presentation outline only after the initial independent attempt and record support. Extension: let a peer supply a new valid case and require a prediction before running. Assess explanation, not decorative slide polish.
teacher.next: Grade 7 is complete when the learner can independently explain and defend the application. Use readiness evidence and recorded support to plan the next level.
